details.text: The pre-industrial custom of "Saint Monday" — where artisans routinely took Monday as an unofficial day off and made up the output later in the week — was so widespread that factories had to be specifically designed to abolish it. The historian E. P. Thompson, whose 1963 book "The Making of the English Working Class" is the landmark study of this transformation, argued that the shift to clock time was as psychologically radical as any other change the Industrial Revolution imposed — ordinary workers experienced it as a form of dispossession.

events.label: The Great Stink of London
events.description: In the summer of 1858, the sewage-choked Thames became so foul in the heat that Parliament — which sits right on the riverbank — could not use its riverside committee rooms. The episode, known as the Great Stink, finally broke political resistance to funding a proper sewer system.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The smell was the product of decades of failure: London's aging sewers emptied directly into the Thames, and the miasma was thought to transmit disease, so the stench was also genuine fear. Curtains were reportedly soaked in chloride of lime to make the Parliamentary chambers bearable, and still MPs fled. Three cholera outbreaks before 1858 had already been blamed on the river — the Great Stink simply put the problem at the precise altitude where money was controlled.

events.label: William Wilberforce
events.description: William Wilberforce was the Yorkshire MP who led Parliament's twenty-year campaign against the Atlantic slave trade — a devout evangelical who turned abolition from a fringe position into an unanswerable moral cause.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Wilberforce introduced an abolition bill in Parliament every year from 1789 onward and was defeated repeatedly before finally winning in 1807. He had intended to press on to full emancipation but poor health forced him to pass leadership to others; he died in 1833, just three days after hearing that Parliament had finally passed the Slavery Abolition Act. His 1785 religious conversion completely reshaped his political priorities — he had been on track for a conventional career as a social and political climber before it.

events.label: Marx and Engels in Manchester and London
events.description: Friedrich Engels ran his family's cotton mill in Manchester — giving him a firsthand view of exactly the system he and Marx were analysing — and used the income to support the perennially broke Marx through decades of research and writing in London. Their collaboration produced Marxism as a working intellectual system, not just a set of pamphlets.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Engels wrote The Condition of the Working Class in England (1845) from his direct observation of Manchester's slums while still in his mid-twenties — a work Marx called the best empirical study of industrial poverty ever written. He maintained a double life in Manchester for years: running the mill by day, attending radical meetings by night, and keeping a working-class partner (Mary Burns, then her sister Lizzie) rather than marrying respectably. When he finally sold his share of the mill in 1869, he moved to London to work full-time with Marx.

events.label: The coal–iron–rail–steam feedback loop
events.description: Railways needed iron and coal; mining and ironmaking needed railways and steam; each drove the others. This self-reinforcing loop was the engine of mid-century growth.

events.label: The electrification of the city
events.description: Electric light, trams, and power transformed work, leisure, and the night in the late-century city. The second wave reached ordinary daily life as the first never quite had.

events.label: Toward the assembly line
events.description: The moving assembly line that Henry Ford perfected in 1913 didn't appear from nowhere — it grew out of interchangeable parts manufacturing (Chapter 16) and the 'disassembly' lines Cincinnati and Chicago meatpackers used to break down carcasses efficiently, the first time a continuous production flow was applied to a complex product.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Chicago meatpackers hung carcasses on overhead rails and moved them past stationary workers, each doing one cut — Ford later said the packinghouses directly inspired his Highland Park line. The assembly line reduced the time to build a Model T from over 12 hours to about 93 minutes. By 1914, Ford was paying workers $5 a day — double the going rate — partly to reduce the brutal turnover the line's monotonous pace caused.

events.label: A divided world
events.description: By 1900 industrial nations were perhaps ten times richer per head than the societies they dominated. The Industrial Revolution's deepest legacy was global inequality.
